@graph.headline: GitHub says agents started more than 40% of PRs
@graph.description: GitHub says agents started over 40% of September PRs. What the signal measures, misses, and how teams can track review outcomes.

mainEntity.name: Does “40% of pull requests” mean AI wrote 40% of all code?

acceptedAnswer.text: No. GitHub says more than 40% of September pull requests started with an agent’s first draft under its detection method. The report does not measure the share of code lines generated by AI, the amount of later human editing, or all AI assistance that may not appear as an agent-started pull request.

mainEntity.name: What does GitHub mean by an agent-started pull request?

acceptedAnswer.text: GitHub describes it as a pull request whose first draft came from a coding agent that the platform can detect. That is a narrower category than any pull request where a developer used AI. It also says the metric is a floor because some agent use may not be detected.

mainEntity.name: Do the merge figures show that agent code is better?

acceptedAnswer.text: No. The report says 90% of agent-started pull requests merged within two weeks in September, compared with about 86% for pull requests without detected agent involvement. That is a descriptive timing comparison, not a measure of correctness, security, maintainability or later defects.

mainEntity.name: How should an engineering team measure its own agent use?

acceptedAnswer.text: Choose one unit and state the denominator, period and detection method. Keep agent-started work separate from human-authored work assisted by a model. Track merge timing, review effort, test failures and post-merge defects as separate outcomes; do not infer quality from throughput alone.

mainEntity.name: Should agent-created pull requests get a different review standard?

acceptedAnswer.text: The cited GitHub guidance recommends human review and testing before agent-generated changes merge, and repository owners can configure required approvals and checks. Teams should set policies based on risk and repository controls, not assume that an agent label makes a change safer or more dangerous by itself.
